8 Transmission system
Vehicles can have various drive arrangements:
Front wheel drive: The driving wheels are located at the front. The advantage of front wheel drive is that all the main components are accommodated under the bonnet thus allowing maximum space within the car for the occupants, without floor bulges for the rear passengers. Using the front wheels for steering allows the driving force to act in the same direction as the wheel is pointing. Mostly, the engine is mounted transversely. This simplifies the transmission, with the clutch and the gearbox mounted in the main unit on the front axle.
Rear wheel drive: The driving wheels are at the back. The normal layout in a rear wheel drive vehicle is, the engine and gearbox at the front and the differential behind.
Four-wheel drive: The drive is distributed to all four wheels. (Also referred to as “x4” vehicles).

1 A public health problem
Moreover, in addition to the human drama, it is important to highlight the enormous economic impact (either directly or indirectly) that occurs as a result of a traffic collision.
Costs derived from road traffic accidents are classified as human, material, healthcare and administrative.
Human costs include the loss of lives, productive capacity and physical and psychological suffering. Material costs consist of damages caused on vehicles and their loads as well as on the road and the environment. Healthcare costs comprise first aid, care and treatment of the wounded, rehabilitation and adaptations. Administrative costs hold those of police officers and firefighters and insurance and services management.
People believe that an accident has little effect on them but the cost is borne by taxpayers. The cost of vehicle insurance is also affected, as premiums are affected by collision data and the cost of accidents.
For these reasons, various international organisations, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), believe that road collisions are a priority public health problem throughout the world.
There is a serious need to work together to reduce the high numbers of dead and seriously injured on the roads.

PASSIVE SAFETY ELEMENTS
 
6 The chassis and body
However, this does not guarantee that in a collision the occupants will not suffer injury. Firstly, occupant safety measures have their limitations (in a crash at very high speed, the deformation of the vehicle can be so extensive that the driver and/or passenger(s) are crushed), and secondly, although the carrier compartment reduces the impact, the sharp acceleration and deceleration that occurs during an accident can cause injuries to the vehicle occupants.
For all these reasons, a highly resistant body can never replace other passive safety systems.
(Página 74 del manual 'Learning to drive')

5 Generic speed        
     
5.3 Minimum generic speed
The generic minimum speed limits, both inside and outside populated areas, are:
On motorways and dual carriageways: 60 km/h for all motor vehicles.
On the remaining roads: the minimum speed is half of the maximum generic speed for each road.
